analysis.one_liner: Restores FCC authority to enforce the 2010 net neutrality rules for broadband providers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A federal court struck down parts of the FCC's 2010 open Internet rules, which stopped broadband companies from blocking or slowing websites. This bill would have written the FCC's authority for those rules directly into law and directed the agency to put the vacated protections back in place within 180 days. It never left the House committee it was assigned to.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet. The bill would have restored rules preventing internet providers from blocking websites or speeding up some sites over others, keeping the internet open to small websites, startups, and ordinary users on equal terms.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes the FCC's authority to adopt the December 2010 open Internet rules into the Telecommunications Act itself, giving the rules a firm legal foundation after a court vacated parts of them.
It requires the FCC, within 180 days of enactment, to take all actions necessary to restore the portions of the 2010 rules struck down by the D.C. Circuit in Verizon v. FCC in January 2014.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband internet providers like cable and phone companies, which would face enforceable limits on blocking, throttling, or selling favored treatment for some websites over others. Any compliance costs could be passed to consumers.

drawbacks.text: The FCC adopted its own new open Internet rules in February 2015 under a different legal approach, so parts of this bill were partly redundant by the time it was introduced; opponents of the 2015 rules argued broadband investment would suffer under heavier regulation.
Locking the 2010 rules into statute would have removed the FCC's flexibility to adapt net neutrality rules to changing technology and future court rulings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to everyday internet users is broad and real: enforceable rules against blocking or slow-lane deals protect small websites and consumers from gatekeeping by their internet provider. The cost falls on broadband companies, which argued regulation discouraged investment, though the rules the bill would restore were relatively modest compared to the stricter Title II approach the FCC later took on its own. On balance, this was a consumer-protection bill whose main cost fell on a concentrated industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote, until the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Peters introduced the Open Internet Act of 2015 on March 17, 2015.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors during its entire life in the 114th Congress.

The bill would have amended Section 706 of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 to authorize the FCC's 2010 open Internet rules and required the FCC to restore the portions vacated by the D.C. Circuit in Verizon v. FCC (decided January 14, 2014) within 180 days of enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers, including large cable and telecom companies, avoided a statutory basis for enforceable open Internet rules; internet users did not get the restored protections this bill offered.

for.name: Rep. Scott H. Peters
for.role: U.S. Representative, California's 52nd District; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Open Internet Act of 2015 to restore the FCC's authority and the vacated 2010 net neutrality rules.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; chair at the time was Rep. Fred Upton (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing, reported it, or advanced it to the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors from either party, so no party split was ever recorded; the bill died in a committee led by Republicans with a lone Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would have restored enforceable rules barring broadband companies from blocking websites or favoring some sites over others, limiting their ability to charge websites for priority delivery. Consumers' internet experience is the product being regulated, so the industry's interest in blocking the rules runs against open access for users.
Restored open Internet rules would prevent providers from charging edge companies for access to customers or degrading their traffic, protecting small sites and services that cannot pay for priority.
